text: Now let's actually work with the team on a real change — end to end, from a vague idea in chat to a merge-ready pull request. Our example: a bank transfer form that today accepts any text in its IBAN field and always reports success. We want it to validate the recipient's IBAN before the transfer can go through.

This is the Agent Chat, where a human talks directly to any agent. On the left is our team with its four members: Business Analyst, Code Reviewer, Developer and Reworker. In the middle is the conversation, and on the right a live view into the agent's own workspace.

I describe the request to the Business Analyst in plain language. And here's the first thing to appreciate: it doesn't just start writing a spec. It looked at the current form and pushes back with the six questions that genuinely need a human decision — when validation happens, what to do on an invalid IBAN, what if the service is down, and more.

Now I answer, point by point — six short answers to six precise questions. The agent did the hard part of figuring out what needs deciding and framed it so my input is fast and unambiguous. I'm steering the outcome without writing a requirements document myself.

With my decisions, the Business Analyst files Issue sixty-five in GitHub. It's written in two layers: a plain-language human section any stakeholder can read, and a full agent section with the problem, scope, and nine testable acceptance criteria for the delivery team.

Here's the human control point. On GitHub I open the labels menu and apply ready. This label is a deliberate human gate — no agent can set it. By adding it, I approve what gets built, and the moment I do, it becomes an event the platform is listening for.

The ready label fired a trigger, and the Developer woke up automatically — no one opened this chat to prompt it. It implemented the whole change on its own: a testable openiban client, the validation states wired into the form, nine passing tests, a green build — then opened Pull Request sixty-nine and labelled it ready-for-review.

Same pattern again: the ready-for-review label woke the Code Reviewer. It checked out the branch, reviewed the full diff in context, and went through the acceptance criteria one by one. Its verdict: all nine met, tests pass, build green — and it applies ready-to-merge, noting that a human performs the merge.

And this is where we land: Pull Request sixty-nine, ready to merge, cleanly closing Issue sixty-five. From a one-line idea in chat, the team produced a well-specified issue, a complete tested implementation, and a reviewed, merge-ready pull request — each hand-off triggered automatically by a label, with the human in control at exactly the two points that matter.
